name: How to Say No
title: How to Say No
answer: Exit criteria are the conditions agreed before a pilot begins that tell a school when to stop using a tool. They matter because they turn a hard, personal decision into one that was already made, protecting teachers, students and the budget from tools that feel good but do not work.

sections.body: This idea addresses the difficulty of saying no to an AI tool once teachers like it and the vendor is friendly. The solution is to agree on exit criteria before the pilot starts, so that if the tool fails to meet them the decision is already settled and nobody has to argue from scratch. Exit criteria protect teachers, students and the budget from tools that feel good but do not work. They make stopping a normal part of the process rather than a conflict.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: The criteria need to be specific rather than general. A tool should stop if the main measure does not improve against the baseline or the comparison group. It should also stop if a serious privacy or safety incident occurs, or if the vendor will not sign the agreement the district needs in order to scale. Another stopping condition is when the tool works only for some students and leaves others, such as students with disabilities or English learners, further behind. The text does not give separate grade band examples.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no study, figure or finding for this idea beyond the mention of Figure 4.7, which lists the exit criteria. It rests on practice rather than research, and the reasoning offered is that agreed criteria make the decision in advance and protect teachers, students and the budget.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits and risks are set out in the text as the conditions that should trigger a stop: the main measure not improving against the baseline or comparison group, a serious privacy or safety incident, a vendor refusing to sign the agreement the district needs to scale, and a tool that helps only some students while leaving others, such as students with disabilities or English learners, further behind. The decision to stop stays with people, and the text says stopping should be reported as openly as scaling. A short note to staff explaining what was tested, what the results were and why the district stopped builds trust in the process, and teachers who see that pilots can end honestly are more willing to volunteer for the next one.
